lesson.title: Degree Beats Coefficient: Comparing Polynomial Growth Rates
lesson.summary: When two polynomials compete for large x, the one with the higher degree always wins eventually, no matter how much smaller its coefficient is, a fact that can be pinned down exactly by finding the crossover point.
lesson.body:
Among polynomials, growth rate as x approaches infinity is governed entirely by degree, not by the size of any coefficient. If p(x) has degree n and q(x) has degree m with n greater than m, then p eventually grows faster than q by any measure: their ratio p(x)/q(x) approaches infinity, and the difference p(x) - q(x) also approaches infinity. If the two polynomials share the same degree, their ratio approaches the ratio of their leading coefficients instead, meaning they grow at comparable, proportional rates rather than one decisively outpacing the other.

This directly extends the idea of a dominant term: just as a single polynomial's own lower-degree terms eventually become negligible next to its leading term, a lower-degree polynomial eventually becomes negligible next to a higher-degree one, however large the lower-degree polynomial's coefficients happen to be. A large coefficient can only buy a temporary lead; it cannot change which polynomial wins in the long run, because the ratio of degrees, not coefficients, decides the outcome as x grows without bound.

Compare f(x) = 1000x^2 and g(x) = x^3. The coefficient 1000 makes f(x) look dramatically larger at first: at x=10, f(10) = 100,000 while g(10) = 1,000, so f is 100 times bigger. At x=100, f(100) = 10,000,000 while g(100) = 1,000,000, so f is still 10 times bigger. But solve for where they meet: setting 1000x^2 = x^3 gives x^3 - 1000x^2 = 0, so x^2(x - 1000) = 0, meaning the two curves cross at x=1000 (ignoring the trivial crossing at x=0). Beyond that point g(x) permanently overtakes f(x): at x=2000, f(2000) = 1000(4,000,000) = 4,000,000,000 while g(2000) = 8,000,000,000, more than double. At x=10,000, f(10,000) = 1000(100,000,000) = 100,000,000,000 while g(10,000) = 1,000,000,000,000, ten times larger, and the gap only keeps widening from there.

Same-degree competitions resolve more gently. Compare f(x) = 4x^3 + 2x and g(x) = 7x^3 - x, both degree 3. The ratio of leading coefficients predicts a limit of 4/7, approximately 0.571. Check at x=1000: f(1000) = 4,000,000,000 + 2,000 = 4,000,002,000, and g(1000) = 7,000,000,000 - 1,000 = 6,999,999,000, so f(1000)/g(1000) is approximately 0.5714, already essentially indistinguishable from 4/7. Unlike the earlier crossover example, no permanent takeover ever happens here; the two polynomials grow at the same order, locked together in roughly the same 4-to-7 proportion forever, however far x extends.

This is the same lesson from comparing growth rates in general, applied specifically inside the family of polynomials: a massive coefficient advantage is only ever temporary, while a degree advantage is permanent. Positioned on the full growth rate hierarchy, polynomials of any degree still lose in the very long run to exponential functions and still beat logarithmic functions, but within the polynomial family itself, the contest always reduces to a simple comparison of the highest exponent present.
